young.html: Lemuel Gulliver is a ship's doctor who keeps getting shipwrecked in very strange places. On his first voyage he wakes up on a beach in Lilliput, tied down by hundreds of threads. The people there are about six inches tall!

To them Gulliver is a giant, the "Man-Mountain." They feed him huge meals and argue about silly things, like which end of a boiled egg to crack: the big end or the little end. Swift was poking fun at how people in his own country quarreled over small things.

On his second voyage Gulliver reaches Brobdingnag, where everyone is as tall as a church steeple, and now he is the tiny one. A kind girl named Glumdalclitch takes care of him like a doll. The giant king listens to Gulliver brag about England and isn't impressed at all.

young.name: gb-gulliver-scale
young.cap: Choose a voyage and compare Gulliver with the people he meets.

young.html: Lilliput math. The Lilliputians are 12 times smaller than Gulliver. Measure a grown-up's height and divide by 12: that's how tall a Lilliputian would be next to them. Cut out a paper Lilliputian that size. Then try it the other way: a Brobdingnagian is 12 times taller. How tall would one be next to you? Would they fit in your house?

full.text: A satire disguised as a travel book

full.html: Jonathan Swift (1667–1745) was an Anglo-Irish clergyman, Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, and the sharpest satirist of his age. Gulliver's Travels (1726) imitates the travel books that were popular then, with maps, measurements and a plain-spoken narrator. Many readers at first took it as a true story. Swift said he wrote it "to vex the world rather than divert it."
Gulliver, about twelve times taller than the Lilliputians, is a marvel and a burden to them. Swift's numbers are careful:

full.text: …the emperor stipulates to allow me a quantity of meat and drink sufficient for the support of 1728 Lilliputians. Some time after, asking a friend at court how they came to fix on that determinate number, he told me that his majesty's mathematicians, having taken the height of my body by the help of a quadrant, and finding it to exceed theirs in proportion of twelve to one, they concluded, from the similarity of their bodies, that mine must contain at least 1728 of theirs…
full.author: Jonathan Swift
full.ed: Travels of Lemuel Gulliver into Several Remote Regions of the World, Farm and Fireside Company, Springfield, Ohio

full.title: The Lilliputians' arithmetic
full.q: If Gulliver is 12 times as tall as a Lilliputian, and the same shape, how many Lilliputians' worth of body is he?
steps: Every length (height, width, depth) is 12 times as great.
Volume grows as length × width × depth: $12 \times 12 \times 12 = 12^3$.

full.html: Lilliput's politics are a small mirror of Britain's: officials win office by rope-dancing; two parties are divided by the height of their shoe heels; and a long war with the island of Blefuscu began over the right end at which to break an egg. Gulliver captures Blefuscu's fleet but refuses to help enslave its people, and he falls out of favor.

Now Gulliver is the small one. The giants' skin looks coarse to him up close, and he fights off rats and wasps. The king hears his proud account of England's government, laws and wars and is shocked. The king's own wisdom is practical:

full.text: And he gave it for his opinion, "That whoever could make two ears of corn, or two blades of grass, to grow upon a spot of ground where only one grew before, would deserve better of mankind, and do more essential service to his country, than the whole race of politicians put together."
full.author: Jonathan Swift
full.ed: Travels of Lemuel Gulliver into Several Remote Regions of the World, Farm and Fireside Company, Springfield, Ohio

full.text: Part III: Laputa and Part IV: the Houyhnhnms

full.html: In Part III Gulliver visits Laputa, a flying island whose rulers are so lost in mathematics and music that servants must flap them with bladders to make them listen, and the Academy of Lagado, where projectors try to extract sunbeams from cucumbers. It mocks learning cut off from common sense. In Part IV he reaches a land ruled by wise, calm horses, the Houyhnhnms, who live by reason, and finds there brutish creatures in human form, the Yahoos. Gulliver comes home disgusted with people and prefers the company of his horses.
Satire holds up human folly to laughter in order to correct it. Swift's method is the change of scale: by making people tiny, huge, or seen through a horse's eyes, he makes the familiar look strange.

Taking Gulliver's view at the end as Swift's own. Many readers think Swift is mocking Gulliver too: he becomes ridiculous in his scorn for his family. Readers still argue about how far Swift shared it.

deep.text: How the book has been read

deep.html: Children have loved Lilliput and Brobdingnag for three centuries, usually in shortened versions. Adult readers have argued over Part IV: is it a hatred of humankind, or a warning against pride, including the pride of thinking we can live by reason alone? Swift wrote to Alexander Pope that he hated "that animal called man" but heartily loved individual people.

Scientists like the book's scale problem. Galileo had already shown (in Two New Sciences, on this ladder) that a giant twelve times taller couldn't simply be a scaled-up person: its weight grows as the cube of its size but the strength of its bones only as the square, so its legs would break. Swift's Brobdingnagians walk about happily anyway.

items: Why might it be easier to see our own faults in a made-up country?
Who is wiser, the king of Brobdingnag or Gulliver?
Is reason alone enough to make a good life, as the Houyhnhnms think?

questions: Which of Gulliver's lands would you most like to visit? Why?
The Lilliputians fought a war over how to crack an egg. What are some silly things people argue about?
How did Gulliver feel when he was the giant? How did he feel when he was the tiny one?
Why do you think the king of Brobdingnag was not impressed by Gulliver's stories about England?
Is it fair to make fun of people to help them see their mistakes?

care: Gulliver's Travels is satire for grown-ups as well as children. A few scenes have rough bodily humor, and the fourth voyage is bitter about human nature. The voyages to Lilliput and Brobdingnag read well aloud with young readers; preview the rest.
